note: A raised, often elaborate structure supporting a coffin or representing one during funeral ceremonies.
short: A raised structure supporting a coffin.

note: One of the solid upright sections of a battlement, between the gaps.
short: A solid upright section of a battlement.

note: A vessel for burning incense, often suspended on chains.
short: A vessel for burning incense.

note: A fine-grained form of silica, often translucent; varieties include agate and carnelian.
short: Fine-grained, often translucent silica.

note: Flashing or sparkling with light.
short: Flashing or sparkling.

note: A monstrous adversary of Zeus in Greek mythology, also called Typhoeus. Hesiod describes him as a son of Earth and Tartarus with a hundred serpent heads. Zeus defeats him with thunderbolts.
short: A many-headed monster opposed to Zeus.

note: A self-moving mechanism or artificial figure. Automata is the Greek-derived plural.
short: A self-moving mechanism or artificial figure.

note: A small room or sleeping chamber; cubicula is the Latin plural.
short: A small room or sleeping chamber.

note: An ancient measure based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
short: An old measure based on the forearm.

note: A spar projecting forward from a ship’s bow, supporting its forward sails and rigging.
short: A spar projecting from a ship’s bow.

note: An extensive, treeless grassy plain of South America.
short: An open South American grassland.

note: A communal dining hall, especially in a monastery or religious house.
short: A communal dining room.

note: A candidate seeking admission to a religious order, before becoming a novice.
short: An applicant for admission to a religious order.

note: A rope used to hoist or lower a sail, flag, or spar.
short: A rope used to raise a sail or flag.

note: A long, low couch, often without a back or arms.
short: A low couch or cushioned seat.

note: A staff carried as an emblem of office, especially a bishop’s pastoral staff.
short: A staff or rod.

note: Showy but worthless finery; things that look impressive without having real value.
short: Worthless showy objects or empty nonsense.

note: Formed from small pieces fitted together, like a mosaic or tiled surface.
short: Formed into a mosaic or tiled pattern.

note: Golden in color or ornamented with gold.
short: Golden or gilded.

note: In a low, quiet voice.
short: In a quiet or lowered voice.

note: A small writing desk with drawers or compartments for papers.
short: A small writing desk.

note: To flash, sparkle, or give off small bursts of light.
short: To sparkle or flash.

note: A metal headband that rises broadest above the forehead and narrows toward the temples, worn in ancient Greece.
short: An ancient Greek metal headband.
An oracle’s shrine.
note: Greek manteion: an oracle, or the sanctuary where a diviner gives an oracular response. The word belongs to the family of mantis, a seer.

short: A wrestling school or exercise court.
note: A palaestra was a place for wrestling and athletic training in ancient Greece or Rome. The Latin word comes from Greek palaistra, related to palē, wrestling. By extension the word can name a school or place of instruction.

short: Possibly Greek: father.
note: Possibly Greek patéra, a form of patéras, father; patéras can also denote a priest.

short: Possibly Greek: mother.
note: Possibly Greek mētéra, mother.

short: A priest who interprets omens.
note: A diviner, especially an official religious interpreter of signs in ancient Rome. Augury sought indications of divine approval or disapproval before an undertaking.

short: A woman credited with prophetic powers.
note: A prophetess through whom a god was believed to speak. Ancient traditions placed sibyls in several regions, including Greece and Italy; the Cumaean Sibyl was especially celebrated.

short: A state or royal treasury.
note: The public treasury or the revenues belonging to a sovereign. Latin fiscus originally meant a basket and came to designate the imperial treasury.

short: Alchemical mercury or a universal remedy.
note: An old alchemical term for mercury, or for a universal remedy.

short: A religious community’s dwelling.
note: A monastery or convent where members live in community, rather than as solitary hermits. The name ultimately combines Greek words for common and life.

short: An assistant, especially to a bishop.
note: A helper or colleague in an office. In church usage, a coadjutor assists a bishop and may hold the right to succeed that bishop.

short: A presiding officer or spokesman.
note: A person appointed to speak for others, or to preside over an assembly. In ecclesiastical usage the title belongs to the chair of a convocation.

short: A principal clerk.
note: The chief clerk of certain courts or other official bodies. The title derives from words meaning first and notary.

short: A basin for washing the hands.
note: A washbasin, especially one supplied from a small tank or vessel above it. Its Latin name means “I shall wash.”

short: Gilt bronze or brass ornament.
note: Bronze or brass given a gold surface and used for decorative objects, furniture mounts, and fittings. The French expression or moulu literally means ground gold.

short: An alloy used for strong permanent magnets.
note: An iron-based magnetic alloy containing aluminum and nickel, with cobalt and sometimes other additions. Its name compresses aluminum, nickel, and cobalt.

short: A watchword or identifying token.
note: In Latin, tessera can mean a military watchword as well as the token or tablet used to communicate or authenticate it.

short: Greek “all” or “whole.”
note: Pas is the masculine singular of the Greek word for all or whole. Its corresponding feminine and neuter forms are pasa and pan.

short: Greek “hawk” or “falcon.”
note: Hierax is an ancient Greek word for a hawk or falcon. Its stem hierak- appears in compounds and related names.

short: A many-headed sea monster of Greek myth.
note: A monster inhabiting the rocks opposite Charybdis. In Homer’s Odyssey she has six heads on long necks and snatches sailors from vessels passing her cave.

short: The abyss beneath the underworld.
note: Tartarus, the deep pit below the realm of the dead in Greek cosmology, also personified as a primordial being. In Hesiod the defeated Titans are confined there.

short: A Siren whose name means “song.”
note: Molpe is one of the Sirens named in the Hesiodic tradition. The Sirens’ alluring song draws passing sailors toward destruction. Her Greek name means song.

short: One of the Sirens of Greek tradition.
note: A Siren named in the account attributed to Apollodorus. The Sirens are supernatural singers whose voices enchant those who hear them.

short: The Greek sphinx.
note: A form of the Greek name for the sphinx: a creature with a lion’s body, a woman’s head, and wings. The Theban sphinx destroyed travelers who could not answer her riddle, until Oedipus solved it.

short: Possibly Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete.
note: Possibly Talos, the bronze giant who guarded Crete in Greek myth. In English, talus also means the ankle bone or a slope of accumulated rock fragments.

short: Irish “wing.”
note: Irish sciathán means a wing; it can also denote a projecting side or extension. Its ending is diminutive.

short: Irish “eagle.”
note: Iolar is the Irish word for an eagle. More specific names combine it with another word, as in iolar mara, a sea eagle.

short: Irish “sun.”
note: Grian is the Irish word for the sun. Its genitive form is gréine, found in expressions describing sunlight or solar things.

short: Irish “wren.”
note: Irish dreoilín means a wren; dreoilín donn names the Eurasian wren. The word is also found in the Irish name for Wren Day.

short: A tassel-flowered plant; also fuzzy yarn.
note: Acalypha hispida, a plant with long, furry-looking clusters of red flowers. Chenille also means a fuzzy yarn or fabric; the French word means caterpillar.

short: A Saharan antelope with spiral horns.
note: A pale-coated desert antelope, Addax nasomaculatus, with long, twisted horns. It is native to the Sahara.

short: A northern diving seabird.
note: A short-necked seabird of the family Alcidae, typically black and white. Auks use their wings underwater while diving; the extinct great auk, unlike living auks, was flightless.

short: An Indonesian wild pig.
note: A babirusa, a wild pig of the genus Babyrousa found in Indonesia. Its name comes from Malay words for pig and deer.

short: The Himalayan blue sheep.
note: A goatlike mountain mammal, Pseudois nayaur, with a gray-blue coat. It inhabits high country in the Himalayas and neighboring parts of Asia.

short: A South American rodent.
note: A member of the rodent family Caviidae, which includes the guinea pigs. Cavies are not rabbits; the name commonly denotes the short-tailed, rough-haired forms.

short: A large, semiaquatic South American rodent.
note: Also called nutria, the coypu has coarse fur and spends much of its time in and around fresh water. Its scientific name is Myocastor coypus.

short: A bushbaby.
note: A galago, or bushbaby, is a small African primate active chiefly at night and at home in trees. Galagos have large eyes and belong to the family Galagidae. The name is used both broadly and as a zoological genus name.

short: A grass-eating Ethiopian monkey.
note: Theropithecus gelada, a large, long-haired monkey resembling a baboon. It is native to Ethiopia and feeds chiefly on grasses.

short: A small Asian goat-antelope.
note: A member of Naemorhedus, a genus of mountain-dwelling bovids ranging from the Himalayan region into China. Gorals combine a goatlike build with antelope-like features.

short: A South American relative of the weasels.
note: A low-slung carnivorous mammal with a gray upper coat and darker underparts. Grisons belong to the weasel family; the name comes from French gris, gray.

short: A small, thickset African or Middle Eastern mammal.
note: A short-legged mammal with small ears, a rudimentary tail, and padded feet with broad nails. Hyraxes are also called dassies or coneys.

short: The anvil-shaped bone of the middle ear.
note: The middle one of the three auditory ossicles, between the malleus and stapes. Its Latin name means anvil, describing its shape.

short: A brilliant Central American trogon.
note: A forest bird with iridescent green upperparts and red underparts. In the resplendent quetzal, the male’s exceptionally long upper tail-coverts extend well beyond the tail itself.

short: A fish with a suction disk on its head.
note: A suckerfish that attaches itself to larger marine animals or other surfaces. The Latin name means delay, from an ancient belief that these fish could hold back a ship.

short: A slow-moving nocturnal primate.
note: A tailless or short-tailed, tree-dwelling primate native to southern Asia. Lorises have large eyes and move deliberately along branches.

short: A nocturnal African tree-dwelling primate.
note: A woolly-coated primate of tropical Africa, with a short tail and a reduced index finger. Pottos move slowly and grip branches firmly.

short: A small, very large-eyed nocturnal primate.
note: A primate of Southeast Asian islands with long hind limbs and a slender tail. Its conspicuously large eyes suit its nocturnal life.

short: A long-legged jumping desert rodent.
note: A small nocturnal rodent of arid parts of Africa and Asia. Its elongated hind legs and long balancing tail support rapid, kangaroo-like leaps.

short: A coarse, naturally brownish wild silk.
note: Silk produced by certain moths other than the domesticated mulberry silkworm. The word, from Hindi and Urdu tasar, also names the moth or caterpillar producing it.

short: A slender, spotted or banded forest mammal.
note: A small, long-tailed carnivore of tropical forests. The name applies to Asian Prionodon and African Poiana, animals resembling civets.

short: A large, spotted American rodent.
note: A nocturnal rodent of tropical America, with a stocky body and rows of pale spots along its flanks.

short: The mountain beaver.
note: Aplodontia rufa, a burrowing rodent of western North America. Mountain beaver is another name for this animal.

short: An African striped polecat.
note: A mustelid with conspicuous black-and-white markings and strong-smelling defensive secretions. The name is also written zorille.

short: The honey badger.
note: Mellivora capensis, a tough-bodied member of the weasel family found in Africa and parts of Asia. Its upper coat is pale and its underside dark.

short: The wolverine’s genus.
note: Gulo is the zoological genus containing the wolverine. The Latin word gulo means a glutton.

short: The swordfish’s genus.
note: Xiphias is the genus of the common swordfish. The Greek name is related to xiphos, a sword.

short: A fly of the blackfly family.
note: A member of the family Simuliidae, the small flies commonly called blackflies. The word comes from the genus Simulium.

short: A parasitic fluke.
note: A parasitic flatworm of the class Trematoda. Many flukes have a flattened body and suckers by which they attach to their hosts.

short: A camel.
note: An Anglo-Indian word for a camel, borrowed from Hindi and Urdu. It is also encountered in Australian usage.

short: The aurochs, an extinct wild ox.
note: An old name for the aurochs, the wild ancestor of domestic cattle. Urus was the Latin name for this animal.

short: Introductory study before interpretation.
note: The preliminary study of a text’s literary and historical background, especially study preparing for the interpretation of the Bible.

short: The study of sacred lore.
note: Related to hierology: religious lore and literature, or the study of sacred things.

short: A fleshy-leaved stonecrop.
note: Hylotelephium telephium, formerly Sedum telephium, is a perennial succulent with clusters of small, star-shaped pink or purplish flowers. It is also called live-forever.

short: An early-flowering daphne shrub.
note: Daphne mezereum bears fragrant rose-purple flowers before its leaves and later produces bright berries. The plant is poisonous.

short: Hebrew “raven.”
note: The Hebrew noun orev means a raven or crow. The older transliteration Oreb preserves a b for the same Hebrew consonant.

short: An ancient name of Aphrodite.
note: Kypris, also written Cypris, is a name of Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty.

short: A half-woman, half-serpent of Greek myth.
note: In Hesiod’s Theogony, Echidna has a nymph’s upper body and an immense snake’s lower body. With Typhon she is the mother of monsters including Cerberus and the Hydra.

short: A person taught by a god.
note: Greek theodidaktos means taught by God, combining theos, god, with didaktos, taught. The adjective appears in 1 Thessalonians 4:9.

short: A visible appearance of a deity.
note: A manifestation in which a god becomes visible. The word comes through Greek theophaneia, combining the divine with the idea of appearing.

short: Spanish “municipal council.”
note: The governing council of a town or city, consisting of its mayor and councillors.

short: Spanish “court of law.”
note: A court or judicial office; also the place where the judge exercises that office.

short: Spanish “shore” or “bank.”
note: The edge of a body of water: the shore of the sea, or the bank of a river or lake.

short: A tree-lined walk or avenue.
note: Spanish alameda originally denotes a grove of poplars; it also names a public walk planted with trees.

short: A bristly-headed plant used in cloth finishing.
note: A plant of the genus Dipsacus. The dried heads of fuller’s teasel have hooked prickles and were used to raise a nap on woven cloth.

short: A genus of molds with rounded spore cases.
note: Mucor is a genus of molds that form fluffy colonies and produce spores in rounded spore cases at the tips of upright stalks.

short: An earthball fungus.
note: Scleroderma is a genus of tough-skinned, puffball-like fungi. Their interior darkens as the spores mature; the fungi form close associations with tree roots.

short: A delicately leaved culinary herb.
note: Anthriscus cerefolium, an aromatic herb of the carrot family. Its divided leaves are used in salads, soups, and other dishes.

short: A genus of succulent plants.
note: A chiefly southern African genus of fleshy-leaved plants. Its name comes from Latin crassus, thick; older botanical usage included certain stonecrops.

short: A microscopic green alga.
note: A member of a group of green algae whose cells are often joined or divided into matching halves. The name derives from Greek desmos, a bond.

short: The number being subtracted.
note: In a subtraction, the subtrahend is the quantity taken away. In 9 minus 4, it is 4; the starting quantity is the minuend.

short: A close-fitting medieval tunic.
note: Also called a jupon: a shirtlike garment, often padded or quilted, worn beneath armor. The word is related to French jupe.

short: A keyboard instrument with wheel-bowed strings.
note: A harpsichord-shaped instrument whose strings sound through contact with revolving wheels, rather than by plucking.

short: A glossy black, red-legged crow relative.
note: A bird of the genus Pyrrhocorax, with dark, glossy plumage and red legs. The English name is pronounced “chuff.”

short: Latin “marshy places.”
note: Palustria is a neuter plural form of the Latin adjective paluster, marshy or swampy. It belongs to the same word family as palus, a marsh.

short: Latin “river” or “stream.”
note: Amnis names flowing water, especially a river or a strong current. Its Latin plural is amnes.

short: Latin “city.”
note: A city or walled town. In Roman usage, urbs without further qualification can mean Rome itself.

short: Greek “pig” or “swine.”
note: Ancient Greek hus, written ὗς, means a pig or hog. The noun can be used of either sex.

short: An earthy deposit rich in lime.
note: Loose or crumbly sediment containing a substantial amount of calcium carbonate, mixed with materials such as clay, sand, or silt.

short: A metal used to strengthen steel.
note: A metallic element, symbol Mo, added to steel for strength and hardness. Its name descends from Greek molybdos, lead.

short: The sage genus.
note: A large genus of herbs and shrubs in the mint family, including culinary sage and many flowering garden plants. The Latin name means sage.

short: A leader of thieves.
note: Old cant for the chief of a group of thieves or vagrants. It combines the approving dimber, “fine,” with damber; historical dictionaries also print it as two words or a hyphenated compound.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A dog.
note: An old cant word for a dog, recorded in Francis Grose’s dictionary of slang.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Food or provisions.
note: Food carried or obtained for a meal. As a verb, prog also means to forage.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Money.
note: An old slang term for money. Historical dictionaries also spell it lowr.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A man or fellow.
note: A cant term for a man. A bob cull is a good-natured fellow.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A woman.
note: An old cant term for a woman, as recorded in Grose’s historical slang dictionary.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A low sighing or moaning sound.
note: A low, continuous sighing, rushing, or moaning sound, especially the sound of wind among trees or through a narrow opening. The verb means to make that sound.

short: Flickering softly or lightly luminous.
note: Playing lightly over a surface, as a small flame does; by extension, softly glowing or radiant. The underlying Latin verb means to lick, an image of flame touching a surface without consuming it.

short: Dry and withered.
note: Dry, withered, or stripped of freshness, especially of vegetation. A literary description of leaves or land, rather than a statement about temperature alone.

short: Possibly Old French: a circle.
note: Possibly Old French viron, a circle or the country round about. It belongs to the family of virer, “to turn,” and environ, “around.”

short: Possibly Termagant, a medieval stage deity.
note: Possibly Termagant, an imaginary deity of medieval European literature. Christian writers wrongly ascribed this figure to Muslims; on the stage the character became a noisy, overbearing tyrant. The later English insult termagant developed from that theatrical tradition.

short: Spanish: a protective wire screen.
note: Spanish alambrera is wire mesh or a protective wire cover, such as a screen over a window or food. It is formed from alambre, wire; the central image is an enclosing barrier.

short: A walrus’s penile bone.
note: An oosik is the baculum, or penile bone, of a walrus. The word comes from Iñupiaq usuk. It names a particular anatomical structure, not the animal as a whole.

short: Irish: air.
note: Irish aer means air, the atmosphere, or the open air. It is the ordinary language word rather than the name of a particular bird.

short: Irish: quick or nimble.
note: Irish mear means quick, nimble, or lively. It can also mean hasty or rash: speed in action can become haste in judgment.

short: Irish: a can or vessel.
note: Irish canna means a can or container. This noun should be distinguished from the Scottish and northern English contraction canna, “cannot.”

short: A small shrine or framed niche.
note: A small shrine or a niche given the architectural form of a little building. The name comes from Latin aedicula, a diminutive of aedes, a house or temple.

short: Latin: a bath or bathing room.
note: Latin balneum means a bath, bathing place, or bathing room. The word was borrowed from Greek balaneion and is the ancestor of English terms beginning balneo-, concerned with baths.

short: Latin: a little dining room.
note: A little dining room. Latin cenatiuncula is a diminutive of cenatio, a room for dining; the diminutive makes the room small or intimate rather than a large banqueting hall.

short: Latin: a school or place of study.
note: Latin schola means a school, lecture, or learned discussion. It comes from Greek scholē, leisure devoted to study: the word’s history links learning with time free from other work.

short: A strong distilled spirit.
note: A strong distilled spirit, related to Portuguese aguardente and Spanish aguardiente. Both names literally describe “burning water”; the word does not specify a single ingredient or fixed strength.

short: Possibly Greek chrēsmos, an oracle or prophetic response.
note: Possibly Greek chrēsmos, an oracle or prophetic response, often delivered in verse.

short: Old cant for pretty or fine.
note: Old cant for pretty, fine, or attractive.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A lantern with a shutter.
note: A dark lantern used in housebreaking, its light concealed when necessary.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A stagecoach or hired carriage.
note: An old abbreviation of diligence, a stagecoach; also used for a post-chaise.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: An insulting word for a bulky woman.
note: An old derogatory term for a fat, awkward, or lazy woman.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Eyes.
note: Slang for eyes, also written glimms. A singular glim can instead mean a candle or lantern.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: To slip something in surreptitiously.
note: An old spelling of foist: to insert secretly or fraudulently, especially with “in.”

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Too much.
note: A cant expression meaning too much, rather than a particular denomination of money.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: To speak pleasantly or civilly.
note: Cant for speaking civilly or ingratiatingly; also recorded as “cut bene whiddes.”

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: An Asian vine with aromatic leaves.
note: Betel is the climbing pepper vine Piper betle, whose leaves are chewed with areca nut. The leaf and the so-called betel nut come from different plants.

short: A flowering plant of the pink family.
note: Campion is a common name for several flowering plants of the pink family, traditionally assigned to Lychnis and Silene. The name does not select one particular species.

short: A plant of the genus Polygala.
note: Milkworts are plants of the genus Polygala. The traditional name reflects an old belief that such plants increased milk production; the name is not a promise of that effect.

short: Possibly asphodel, a flower associated with the Greek underworld.
note: Possibly asphodel, a plant of the genus Asphodelus with tall spikes of pale flowers. In Homer’s Odyssey, the spirits of the dead inhabit a meadow of asphodel.

short: Possibly the martagon lily.
note: Possibly martagon, a lily with petals that curl backward into a turban-like shape.

short: A stand or frame for a coffin.
note: A frame or stand on which a dead body or coffin is carried or displayed. The word is related to bear in the sense of carrying a weight.

short: A railing supported by small pillars.
note: A row of small pillars, called balusters, supporting a rail. The term names the whole barrier along a stair, balcony, or terrace, rather than one of its supports.

short: Funeral rites or observances.
note: The ceremonies performed for someone who has died. The word is normally plural and concerns the observances surrounding burial, rather than the grave itself.

short: A thick, softly napped cloth.
note: A woolen or cotton cloth with a felt-like surface. It is commonly used to cover gaming tables and to line or cover doors, where its thickness helps soften noise.

short: Silkworm fiber.
note: The fine fiber spun by silkworms and used to make cloth. The word also denotes the threadlike styles of an ear of corn.

short: An animal’s horn; a hard natural material.
note: An animal’s projecting horn, or its hard outer material. In cattle, a horn has a bony core covered with keratin.

short: A tiny anatomical projection.
note: A small projecting anatomical structure, especially one of the fingerlike projections lining the small intestine. Latin villus means shaggy hair.

short: A plant with stinging hairs.
note: A plant, especially of the genus Urtica, bearing hairs that sting the skin. As a verb, nettle means to irritate or provoke.

short: A fragrant bulb; also a name with a Greek flower myth.
note: A fragrant bulbous plant, especially Hyacinthus orientalis; also an old gemstone name. In Greek myth, Apollo’s beloved Hyacinthus died after a discus struck him, and a flower grew from his blood.

short: A polishable metamorphic rock.
note: Limestone transformed by heat and pressure into crystalline rock, widely used for sculpture and buildings.

short: A predatory freshwater fish.
note: A long-bodied freshwater fish with prominent teeth. Pike also denotes a long thrusting spear.

short: An animal scent used in perfumery.
note: A strongly scented secretion of the male musk deer; also similar fragrances and their substitutes.

short: An aromatic herb with a Greek transformation myth.
note: An aromatic herb of the genus Mentha, including peppermint and spearmint. In Greek myth, the nymph Menthe was transformed by Persephone into fragrant mint.

short: A flowering shrub of the genus Rosa.
note: A shrub of the genus Rosa, or its flower, commonly bearing prickles and fragrant blossoms.

short: A tendon; figuratively, strength.
note: A tendon: the tough tissue joining muscle to bone. Figuratively, bodily strength or a source of strength.

short: A song or expression of praise.
note: A celebratory song of praise or thanksgiving; by extension, an enthusiastic tribute. The word comes from Greek hymns associated with Apollo.

short: Worn or haggard in appearance.
note: Looking worn down, exhausted, or damaged, especially in the face. It describes an appearance rather than a particular illness.

short: Possibly Greek: a lake or pool.
note: Possibly Greek límnē, a lake, pool, or marsh.

short: Possibly Spanish alcalde: mayor.
note: Possibly Spanish alcalde, a mayor or municipal magistrate, from Arabic al-qāḍī, the judge.

short: A spiral, coil, or ring.
note: A spiral or coil; also an arrangement of leaves, petals, or other parts in a ring around an axis.

short: A stone used as a hammer.
note: A stone used for pounding or striking, especially a prehistoric tool used to shape other stones.

short: A small freshwater fish.
note: A small freshwater fish of the carp family, especially the European Leuciscus leuciscus; the name also applies to several North American fishes.

short: A large ground-dwelling bird.
note: A large bird of the family Otididae, found in open country in the Old World and Australia and spending much of its time on the ground.

short: A tropical American forest bird.
note: A large, mostly tree-dwelling bird of the family Cracidae, related to curassows and chachalacas and resembling a slender turkey.

short: A sea eagle.
note: An old word for an eagle, especially the white-tailed sea eagle, Haliaeetus albicilla.

short: A large African antelope.
note: Either of two large African antelopes with spirally twisted horns.

short: A male cat, especially a castrated one.
note: An old word for a male cat, particularly a castrated male. It originated as a familiar form of the name Gilbert.

short: A layered metamorphic rock.
note: A metamorphic rock whose aligned mineral grains allow it to split along roughly parallel layers.

short: A fine-grained sedimentary rock.
note: A sedimentary rock formed from clay or mud, typically splitting into thin layers.

short: Of a palace; possessing royal privileges.
note: Connected with an imperial palace or endowed with royal authority. As a noun, a high palace official or a lord exercising sovereign powers in a territory.

short: A queen or a raja’s wife.
note: A queen in South Asia, or the wife of a raja. From Hindi and Urdu rānī, ultimately Sanskrit rājñī.

short: A large American shorebird.
note: A stocky shorebird with long legs, a straight bill, and striking black-and-white wing markings.

short: Possibly Irish: a leech or vampire.
note: Possibly Irish súmaire, a bloodsucker, leech, or vampire; figuratively, a parasite or sponger.

short: Possibly Semele’s divine name.
note: Possibly Thyone, the name of Semele after her elevation to divine status in Greek myth. Semele was the mother of Dionysus.

short: Possibly the Crommyonian Sow.
note: Possibly Phaea, the fierce Crommyonian Sow killed by Theseus in Greek myth.

short: Possibly Saint Mamelta, a Persian martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Mamelta, also called Memelchtha, a fourth-century Persian martyr. Christian tradition describes a priestess of Artemis who converted to Christianity and was stoned.

short: Possibly Arabic siyūf, swords.
note: Possibly Arabic siyūf, swords, a dialectal plural of sayf or sēf, a sword.

sources.label: Willmore, The Spoken Arabic of Egypt (Birzeit University)

short: Possibly Arabic ṣabā, the east wind.
note: Possibly Arabic ṣabā, the east wind; in Arabic and Urdu literary usage, a gentle morning breeze.

short: Possibly Persian and Urdu sirka, vinegar.
note: Possibly sirka, vinegar, a Persian word also used in Urdu and Hindi.

short: Possibly Arabic banj, an anesthetic.
note: Possibly Arabic banj, an anesthetic or narcotic; the word also names henbane, a plant historically used for its intoxicating effects.

sources.label: Hans Wehr, A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic

short: Possibly Arabic hadīl, a dove’s cooing.
note: Possibly Arabic hadīl, the cooing of a dove. The word is also used as a personal name.

sources.label: Suzanne Pinckney Stetkevych, The Cooing of the Dove and the Cawing of the Crow

short: Possibly Arabic ḥiṣān, a horse or stallion.
note: Possibly Arabic ḥiṣān, a horse or stallion.

short: Possibly Arabic maṭar, rain.
note: Possibly Arabic maṭar, rain. Its plural is amṭār.

short: Possibly Arabic lijām, a bridle.
note: Possibly Arabic lijām, a bridle or rein; the word is also used in Urdu.

sources.label: SOAS: The Provenance of Arabic Loan-words in Hausa

short: Irish gleacaíocht: wrestling, fighting, or gymnastics.
note: Irish gleacaíocht means wrestling or fighting; it also denotes gymnastics, acrobatics, or trickery.

short: A faithful companion, from Virgil’s Achates.
note: Achates is Aeneas’s trusted companion in Virgil’s Aeneid; his name became a term for a loyal friend.

short: A Madagascan primate; its name derives from Latin spirits of the dead.
note: A primate of Madagascar and nearby islands. Its zoological name derives from Latin lemures, spirits of the dead, originally applied by Linnaeus to animals that wandered at night.

short: A stoat, especially in its white winter coat.
note: A stoat or related weasel whose fur turns white in winter while the tail-tip stays black; also its fur, traditionally used to trim ceremonial robes.

short: A small South American monkey; also a name for certain trees.
note: A small, thick-furred South American monkey with a tail that does not grasp. The same spelling also names trees of the southeastern United States, including Cliftonia monophylla.

short: Whale skin and attached blubber eaten in Greenland.
note: A Greenlandic food made from whale skin with its attached layer of blubber.

short: A water opossum of South America.
note: The aquatic opossum Chironectes minimus. Its name comes from the Oyapock River in northern South America.

short: A sea robin; the name is related to grunting.
note: A sea robin, a marine fish. The name comes through French from a verb meaning to grunt.

short: A small deer with unbranched antlers.
note: Any of several small Central and South American deer with simple, unbranched antlers. The older English word also names a young male red deer.

short: A caddisfly or its aquatic larva.
note: A caddisfly or caddisworm. Caddis is also an old term for worsted yarn or the woven binding used for garters.

short: An African forest antelope with white stripes.
note: A large African antelope, Tragelaphus eurycerus, with a reddish chestnut coat crossed by narrow white stripes.

short: A small freshwater fish related to carp.
note: A small freshwater fish of the Old World, belonging to a group closely related to the carps.

short: A woody climbing vine of tropical forests.
note: A climbing vine, usually woody, rooted in the soil and growing up other plants; especially characteristic of tropical rainforests.

short: A name for marsh marigold and related buttercups.
note: A common name for plants of the buttercup family, especially the marsh marigold.

short: The Swiss stone pine.
note: The Swiss pine, also called arolla pine. The name comes from the French dialect of the canton of Valais in Switzerland.

short: A dialect word for a small dog.
note: A dialect word for a small dog, also spelled fice or fyce.

short: A large burrowing rodent of the squirrel family.
note: A stout, short-legged rodent of the genus Marmota, in the squirrel family. Marmots live in burrows and hibernate through winter.

short: An Atlantic porgy with a Narragansett-derived name.
note: Stenotomus chrysops, a porgy found along the Atlantic coast of North America. The English name is shortened from a Narragansett word.

short: A usually small lizard of the family Scincidae.
note: A lizard of the family Scincidae, typically small and insect-eating with an elongated body.

short: A slender carnivorous mammal; also its musky secretion.
note: An Old World carnivorous mammal of the family Viverridae. Civet also names a strong-smelling glandular secretion formerly used in perfume.

short: An Ottoman regular soldier; also the title of Hyderabad’s rulers.
note: A term for regular Ottoman troops or a soldier in that army, from Arabic niẓām, order or organization. Nizam was also the title of the rulers of Hyderabad.

short: Possibly the magical herb in the Odyssey.
note: Possibly the magical herb Hermes gives Odysseus against Circe’s enchantments in the Odyssey. Homer describes a black root and white flowers.

short: Possibly catachresis, an unusual or improper use of a word.
note: Possibly catachresis: using a word in an improper or strained way, or making a deliberately incongruous figure of speech. The Greek root katachrēsis means misuse.

short: A brownish red variety of chalcedony.
note: A brownish red variety of chalcedony, sometimes classed as a kind of carnelian.

short: The Latin form of Ganymede.
note: Catamitus is a Latin form of Ganymede, the beautiful youth of Greek mythology, transmitted through Etruscan Catmite. It is the origin of the English word catamite.

short: A band worn around the head or across the breasts.
note: A narrow band of cloth worn around the hair or, as a garment, around the breasts. French bandeau is a diminutive of bande, band.

short: A flowering plant whose name is Greek for star.
note: A plant of Aster or related genera, bearing flower heads with radiating petals. The name comes from Greek astēr, star.

short: Manioc, a tropical crop grown for its starchy roots.
note: Manihot esculenta, a tropical plant cultivated for its starch-rich roots; also called manioc or yuca.

short: An Asian flowering shrub named for William Kerr.
note: Kerria japonica, an Asian shrub of the rose family with yellow flowers. The genus is named for the gardener William Kerr.

short: Possibly Elodea, a genus of aquatic plants.
note: Possibly Elodea, a genus of submerged aquatic plants. Its name derives from Greek helōdēs, marshy.

short: A name for woody vines, including a poisonous nightshade.
note: A common name for several climbing plants, including Solanum dulcamara, the poisonous bittersweet nightshade, and Celastrus scandens, American bittersweet.

short: A flowering plant of the family Orchidaceae.
note: A plant of the family Orchidaceae. Orchid flowers typically have three petals, with one enlarged into a distinctive lip.

short: A fine-grained metamorphic rock that splits into sheets.
note: A dense, fine-grained rock formed when sediments such as shale are altered by pressure. Its cleavage allows it to split into thin plates.

short: Possibly kurbash, a hide whip.
note: Possibly kurbash, also spelled kourbash, a whip made of hide and used for punishment. The English word comes from Turkish kırbaç.

short: Possibly Allah, the Arabic name for God.
note: Possibly Allah, the Arabic name for God.

short: Latin for a fox.
note: Latin vulpes means a fox; figuratively, cunning or craftiness.

sources.label: Lewis and Short Latin Dictionary, Perseus

short: Latin for an eagle, also a Roman legion’s standard.
note: Latin aquila means an eagle. It also names the eagle-shaped standard of a Roman legion and the constellation of the Eagle.

sources.label: Lewis and Short Latin Dictionary, Perseus

short: A Greek sea goddess and the mother of Achilles.
note: A Nereid, or sea nymph, in Greek mythology. With the mortal Peleus she is the mother of Achilles.

sources.label: Homer and other ancient sources collected at Theoi

short: A cold-water seabird related to petrels.
note: A seabird of the genus Fulmarus, related to petrels. Northern and southern species inhabit the colder seas of their respective hemispheres.

short: A tiny kinglet with a bright yellow crown.
note: Regulus regulus, a very small Eurasian bird with a yellow crown patch bordered by black.

short: A predatory songbird that often impales its prey.
note: A bird of the family Laniidae, with a hooked bill. Shrikes often fasten captured insects or other prey onto thorns.

short: An old word for a leopard.
note: An old word for a leopard, from Latin pardus and Greek pardos. A separate dialect word pard means a partner or friend.

short: A newt, especially in its land-dwelling stage.
note: An old English name for a newt, especially the juvenile phase that lives on land before returning to water.

short: A mature male red deer.
note: A male red deer, especially one older than five years. The word descends from a Germanic expression for a horned animal.

short: An African wildcat with long legs and large ears.
note: Leptailurus serval, an African cat with very long legs, large ears, and black spots on a tawny coat.

short: Large wild cattle with a shoulder hump.
note: Large wild cattle of the genus Bison, with heavy forequarters, a shoulder hump, and a shaggy coat. Living species are native to North America and Europe.

short: A large African monkey with a brightly colored muzzle.
note: Mandrillus sphinx, a large monkey of central Africa. Adult males have striking blue ridges and a red stripe along the muzzle.

short: A flowering plant of the genus Campanula.
note: A plant of the genus Campanula, named for its bell-shaped flowers.

short: A flowering plant named for the botanist Anders Dahl.
note: A plant of the genus Dahlia, in the daisy family, with tuberous roots and showy flower heads. The genus is named for the Swedish botanist Anders Dahl.

short: An aromatic plant of the daisy family.
note: A name for aromatic, daisy-like plants, especially Chamaemelum nobile and Matricaria chamomilla. Their dried flowers are used to make herbal tea.

short: A name for shrubs of the genus Philadelphus.
note: A common name for Philadelphus shrubs, which bear showy white flowers. The name is also applied to several unrelated plants.

short: The entrance vestibule of a church.
note: A vestibule or porch at the entrance of a church, leading into the nave.

short: A Turkish sword with a curved blade and no handguard.
note: A long knife or short saber, usually with a curved cutting edge and no handguard; from Turkish yatağan.

short: A shadow-picture, especially a radiograph.
note: A shadowlike image, especially an X-ray photograph. Its Greek roots are skia, shadow, and graphein, to draw or describe.

short: A name for the sea otter.
note: A name for the sea otter, Enhydra lutris, also used in Russian and German.

sources.label: IUCN: Otters, An Action Plan for their Conservation

short: A cushion-forming plant with pointed leaves.
note: A common name for Acantholimon plants, including A. glumaceum, which forms low cushions of stiff, pointed leaves and bears small pink flowers.

short: Possibly moor-grass, a tufted grass with purple flower clusters.
note: Possibly moor-grass, especially Molinia caerulea, a tufted perennial grass with narrow leaves and purplish flower clusters.

short: Possibly Oregon grapeholly, Mahonia aquifolium.
note: Possibly Mahonia aquifolium, Oregon grapeholly: an evergreen shrub of the Pacific Northwest, with yellow flowers and grape-like fruits.

short: The Greek goddess of retribution.
note: The Greek goddess of retributive justice. Her name also became an English word for a bringer of vengeance or an implacable opponent.

short: Possibly the Exmoor pony, a native British breed.
note: Possibly the Exmoor pony, a native British breed whose herds graze the open moorland of Exmoor. It develops a thick protective winter coat.

short: Possibly Arabic rimāḥ, spears.
note: Possibly Arabic rimāḥ, spears, the plural of rumḥ. The word is also used in Urdu.

short: Possibly Arabic burāz, excrement.
note: Possibly Arabic burāz, excrement or feces.

short: An Arabic greeting meaning welcome.
note: Arabic marḥabā, welcome or hail; also used as an exclamation of approval.

short: Latin for a sitting room furnished with seats.
note: Latin sellaria, a room furnished with seats or couches: a sitting room or drawing room. It derives from sella, a seat.

short: Possibly Latin auscultator, a listener.
note: Possibly Latin auscultator, a listener or one who heeds, from auscultare, to listen.

short: Latin for a seat, throne, or dwelling place.
note: Latin sedes means a seat, bench, or throne; by extension, an abode, residence, or temple.

sources.label: Lewis and Short Latin Dictionary, Perseus

short: Old cant for a bullying fighter or bravo.
note: An old cant word for a swaggering fighter, bully, or knife-wielding bravo; also called Captain Hackum.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: A low, rounded dome with a shallow, cap-shaped profile.
short: A shallow, cap-shaped dome.

note: A medieval trumpet with a piercing tone. As an adjective, clear, loud, and ringing, like a trumpet’s call.
short: A shrill trumpet; also clear and ringing.
Possibly Arabic sajjāda, a prayer rug.
note: Possibly Arabic sajjāda, a rug or mat used for prostration during Muslim prayer. The related verb sajada means to prostrate oneself.

short: Possibly Arabic silāḥ, a weapon or arms.
note: Possibly Arabic silāḥ, a weapon, arms, or military equipment; its plural is asliḥa.

short: Possibly Ganymeda, an ancient name for Hebe.
note: Possibly Ganymeda, the name under which the Greek goddess Hebe was worshipped at Phlius. Hebe was cupbearer to the gods and wife of Heracles.

short: The spider-lily genus; Greek for beautiful membrane.
note: A genus of bulbous American plants in the amaryllis family, commonly called spider lilies. The name combines Greek hymēn, membrane, and kalos, beautiful, referring to the flower’s central cup.

short: Magnesium oxide, a white heat-resistant compound.
note: Magnesium oxide, MgO, a white compound used in heat-resistant materials, cements, and insulation.

short: Possibly Ur, the ancient Sumerian city.
note: Possibly Ur, a Sumerian city in southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq. Its principal deity was the moon god Nanna.

sources.label: Penn Museum · Ur and Its Treasures

short: Liatris, also called blazing-star.
note: A common name for Liatris, or blazing-star: North American plants of the daisy family, often bearing dense clusters of purple flowers.

short: A monkey of the genus Macaca.
note: A monkey of the genus Macaca, a chiefly Asian group with sturdy bodies and tails ranging from long to almost absent.

short: A slender woodland mammal of the weasel family.
note: A carnivorous mammal of the genus Martes, with a slender body and thick fur. Martens inhabit northern forests and are agile tree climbers.

short: The thighbone; Latin femur means thigh.
note: The thighbone, extending from hip to knee; femur is Latin for thigh. In insect anatomy the same word names a major segment of the leg.

short: A small lizard, usually active at night.
note: A small, chiefly tropical lizard. Many geckos hunt insects at night.

short: A name for several kinds of freshwater and marine fish.
note: The European bream, Abramis brama, is a deep-bodied freshwater fish of the carp family. Bream also names sea breams and certain freshwater sunfishes.

short: Corvus frugilegus, a crow that nests in colonies.
note: An Old World crow, Corvus frugilegus, which commonly builds nests in large groups in trees.

short: An Ilex shrub or tree, often with red berries.
note: A shrub or tree of the genus Ilex. Familiar hollies have evergreen leaves with prickly margins and bright red berries.

short: A succulent plant with thick, fleshy leaves.
note: A plant of the genus Aloe, a chiefly African group of succulents with rosettes of thick leaves and spikes or clusters of tubular flowers.

short: Linum, the plant that supplies linen fibre and linseed.
note: A plant of the genus Linum. Common flax, Linum usitatissimum, has blue flowers and is grown for its stem fibres and oil-bearing seeds.

short: Possibly Arabic ʿishsh, a nest.
note: Possibly Arabic ʿishsh, a nest, especially a bird’s nest.

sources.label: H. F. S. Amery, English–Arabic Vocabulary (1905) · nest

short: Arabic: Do you understand Arabic?
note: An Arabic question meaning Do you understand Arabic? The verb is a colloquial form of fahima, to understand; ʿarabī means Arabic.

sources.label: Defense Language Institute · Saudi Arabic Headstart, Module I Lesson 2
Open Linguistics · colloquial Arabic bi-tifham ʿarabi

short: Spanish for chief or boss.
note: Spanish for a chief, leader, or person in command. The word comes through French chef.

short: Old cant for mad or insane.
note: An old cant adjective meaning mad or insane. An Abram-man was a wandering beggar who pretended to be mentally ill to obtain alms.

sources.label: Farmer and Henley, Slang and Its Analogues · Abraham-man
Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Old cant: to go or depart.
note: A verb in historical thieves’ cant meaning to go or leave; bing avast meant to go away.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A group’s private vocabulary; also insincere talk.
note: The specialized speech of thieves, beggars, or another social group, often intended to be opaque to outsiders. Cant can also mean affected or insincere talk.

short: A fool or easily deceived person.
note: An old cant word for a fool or dupe, especially someone readily cheated out of money. Related cull and cully also serve as familiar terms for a man or fellow.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Old cant for a young woman.
note: A historical cant term for a girl or young woman, especially among itinerant or criminal communities; it could also refer to a prostitute.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A rough bed; to sleep or bed down.
note: British slang for a makeshift bed or lodging, and a verb meaning to sleep or settle down for the night.

short: Old slang for chatter, humbug, or deceptive talk.
note: An old slang word for talk or chatter, especially nonsense or deception; as a verb, to fool someone or pretend.

short: A short sword, formerly carried by sailors.
note: A short sword worn at the side, historically used by sailors.

short: Old slang for a miserly person.
note: A contemptuous historical term for a stingy, mean-spirited person.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: An old word for a privy or toilet.
note: An old English name for a privy or latrine.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A lock-pick or false key in thieves’ cant.
note: A historical thieves’ term for a picklock: a tool or false key used to open a lock without its proper key.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A house or lodging in old thieves’ cant.
note: An old cant word for a house, particularly a lodging or meeting place used by thieves and other itinerant people.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Drinks alcohol, in old slang.
note: The verb lush means to drink alcohol. Historical slang also used lush as a noun for strong beer.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: To act as an informer.
note: To inform on someone or give evidence against accomplices. In old criminal cant, a nose was an informer.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Possibly padding-ken, a lodging-house used by thieves.
note: Possibly a shortened form of padding-ken, a low lodging-house frequented by thieves. Ken was cant for a house, and pad could mean to travel on foot or rob on the road.

short: Cheap or poor-quality wine.
note: A colloquial term for cheap, inferior wine, especially in British and Australian English.

short: Possibly putz, a Yiddish-derived insult for a fool.
note: Possibly putz, an English insult borrowed from Yiddish for a foolish, ineffectual, or objectionable person; it is also a vulgar term for the penis.

short: The genuine article; something of the best quality.
note: An older colloquial phrase for the real thing, or a person or object of exceptional quality.

sources.label: Farmer and Henley, Slang and Its Analogues · pure quill

short: Possibly scavey: knowledge, sense, or understanding.
note: Possibly scavey, an older spelling related to savvy: knowledge or practical understanding, also used as a verb meaning to know.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A short upright tail, as on a rabbit or hare.
note: The short tail of a rabbit, hare, or similar animal.

short: To obtain by stealth or irregular means.
note: An informal verb meaning to seize, pilfer, or acquire something by devious means.

short: Old cant: to snooze or sleep.
note: A historical variant of snooze, meaning to sleep.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A dialect spelling of soldier.
note: A colloquial spelling of soldier, also found as sodger or soger in Scots and regional English.

short: To notice, recognize, or understand.
note: An informal verb meaning to observe or catch on to something. Historical cant used twig for noticing a person or seeing through a situation.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A dismissive word for a child or young woman.
note: An old term for a child, or an impudent young woman; it descends from Middle English chitte, a kitten or cub.

short: Money; from German, Dutch, and Yiddish forms.
note: A colloquial word for money, related to German and Dutch geld and Yiddish gelt.

short: Watchful, suspicious, or inquisitive.
note: An old cant adjective for being suspicious, observant, or alert to possible danger.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A flowering bulb; also pure or unsullied.
note: A name for various flowering plants, especially Lilium, with its scaly bulbs and conspicuous flowers. As an adjective, lily can mean pure or unsullied, as in the phrase lily truth.

short: An old term for citizens or townspeople.
note: A plural of cit, an old shortened form of citizen, particularly a resident of London.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A cavalry standard-bearer; also a brass instrument.
note: Historically, a junior cavalry officer who carried the troop’s standard, or the standard itself. Cornet also names a trumpet-like musical instrument.

short: A swift falcon; also wandering or foreign.
note: A peregrine falcon, Falco peregrinus, a widely distributed bird of prey. As an adjective, peregrine means wandering or coming from abroad.

short: Pregnant; figuratively full or heavy with meaning.
note: Pregnant or carrying eggs; figuratively full, teeming, or laden with meaning. The word comes from Latin gravidus, related to gravis, heavy.

short: A thick-rinded citrus fruit.
note: A large aromatic citrus fruit, Citrus medica, whose thick rind is often candied; also the tree bearing it.

short: A twilled fabric traditionally made of silk and worsted wool.
note: Bombazine is a twill fabric traditionally woven with silk threads lengthwise and worsted wool crosswise. The name also denotes a black silk twill.

short: A small skin- or fabric-covered boat.
note: A coracle is a small, lightweight boat made from a framework covered with hide or waterproof fabric. The word comes from Welsh corwgl.

short: A metal vessel holding a lighted fire.
note: A cresset is a metal cup or basket that holds burning fuel for illumination, mounted on a pole or hung like a lantern.

short: The gaps between a battlement’s raised sections.
note: Crenels are the gaps between the raised sections of a battlement. The raised sections are called merlons.

short: Greenish or becoming green.
note: Virescent means greenish or becoming green. It comes from Latin virescere, to grow green.

short: A delicately balanced rock that can be made to sway.
note: A logan stone is a large rock balanced so delicately on its base that a small force can make it sway. It is also called a rocking stone.
